articles.title_orig: Dow futures slide 200 points weighed by Home Depot; traders await Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures slide 200 points weighed by Home Depot; traders await Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.
With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.
Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.
"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.
Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.
The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.
One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.
With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.
By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.
Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

articles.title_orig: Duffy wants $50 billion to avert another ground stop. Experts say money isn’t the issue.
articles.title_zh: Duffy wants $50 billion to avert another ground stop. Experts say money isn’t the issue.
articles.content_orig:

An equipment upgrade appears to have brought airline departures across the U.S. to a standstill Friday , raising questions about how the nation’s air traffic control network is being modernized — and whether safeguards should have prevented the disruption.
The nationwide ground stop — the longest since the September 11 attacks — led to 14,000 flights cancellations Friday and Saturday as the disruption and its aftermath spread through airline schedules. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed an “incredibly old air traffic control system,” saying communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and “went down.” By Saturday, he pointed more specifically to routine work replacing copper telecommunications wiring with fiber .
Aviation experts said precautions should have prevented an equipment change from overwhelming the network, leading to scrutiny over installation procedures and preparations for recovering when an upgrade goes wrong.
The disruption has also intensified a funding debate , with Duffy seeking another $50 billion after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. But experts caution that new equipment alone cannot eliminate failures in a sprawling system that must remain operational throughout its overhaul.
“A large-scale modernization, no matter how warranted and well-intended, cannot solve all these problems. This is a system that runs 24/7, 365 days a year. We cannot turn it off while we build a new one and then start a new one from scratch,” David Lovell, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Maryland, told The Independent .
“Any modernization will, by necessity, be done piecemeal. That will mean integrating new subsystems with old subsystems, with the consequent interfaces at the boundaries that are often points of vulnerability,” he added.
Air traffic controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and aircraft communications at 3:36 p.m. Friday, Duffy said. Eighteen minutes later, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop , barring departures as officials sought to identify the problem.
The order was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but airlines continued struggling to restore their schedules. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, with thousands more canceled or delayed Saturday, leaving thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the U.S.
Duffy said Saturday that contractor L3Harris may have installed a faulty router — a device that directs information through a network — at a site in Arkansas . The work involved replacing copper wires, which carry electrical signals, with fiber optic cables, which can transmit more data over longer distances.
L3Harris has partnered with the federal government for a decade and is replacing the Federal Aviation Administration’s copper wires with fiber-optic cables. FAA and company officials are working in L3Harris’ Florida lab to analyze the router at the center of the stop.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” the company said in a statement.
The company’s work comes the nation has long sought to upgrade its decade-old air traffic control system. Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, Florida, told Time Magazine that billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
An overload can affect facilities around the country that exchange radar information and voice communications, said Hassan Shahidi, president and CEO of the Flight Safety Foundation.
“It appears to have been a system overload caused by this new router,” he told The Independent .
Lance Sherry, a professor of systems engineering at George Mason University, said air traffic control comprises three interacting networks: communications, navigation and surveillance. Their connections help explain how a local problem can spread to a nationwide shutdown.
“For this reason we consider [air traffic control] to be a network-of-networks,” Sherry said. “A perturbation in one location of the network can, under the right circumstances, propagate through the network.”
Independent industry analyst Bob Mann noted that the FAA had recently expanded its SMART traffic-management platform nationwide. The AI-assisted tool, which helps FAA staff plan traffic flows, was rolled out nationally three days before the ground stop.
Federal officials, however, have said this new tool was not responsible for the outage.
Lovell said the disruption should not obscure the safety response.
“The safety aspects of the system performed admirably,” he told The Independent . “The procedures to get aircraft out of the air safely worked perfectly, and there was no loss of life or bodily injury.”
The FAA and its telecommunications provider should have safeguards to prevent an equipment change from overwhelming the network, Shahidi said. Preliminary findings pointed to a router setting that apparently allowed it to send excessive information.
“This particular router has a feature that has a broader broadcast capability. That feature apparently was not disabled,” he said.
While investigators were still establishing the cause, he argued that appropriate settings, testing and training should block such an overload. “This is something that I believe is preventable,” he said.
The FAA has already replaced more than 3,500 copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections, out of 5,170 scheduled for replacement by 2028.
With many more upgrades ahead, Shahidi said understanding what went wrong and preparing for future installations is essential. “They need to have a plan, a backup plan,” he said.
The disruption has sharpened a dispute over whether the FAA needs more money or a better plan for spending what it already has. The administration says existing funding cannot cover a full overhaul, while Democrats are demanding an accounting of unspent money and a clearer explanation of what another $50 billion would buy.
Congress approved $12.5 billion for modernization last year, which Duffy has described as a down payment rather than the full cost of replacing outdated systems. By Friday, he increased that request to $50 billion, calling the need an “emergency.”
“This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said Friday.
President Donald Trump took a more partisan approach in Sunday Truth Social posts, accusing the Biden administration of making an “ old and broken system worse than when they began .” He urged Congress to approve funding rather than modernizing in “drips and drabs.”
Democrats say their objections are not to modernization itself, but to the administration’s management of the effort. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said previously approved funding largely remained unspent and accused Duffy of demanding “a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver.”
“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner,” she said in a statement.
Beyond the funding dispute lies a separate question: whether replacing old equipment would prevent another disruption similar to Friday’s. Lovell said the suspected involvement of newly installed routers complicated that argument.

articles.title_orig: What does Huang's ouster mean for the global AI race?
articles.title_zh: What does Huang's ouster mean for the global AI race?
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023.
Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars.
Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable.
Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in.
Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history.
The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.
What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China.
The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

articles.title_orig: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.title_zh: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump inspects an honor guard after stepping off Air Force One, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila, Philippines. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.
Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.
The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.
Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Firdia Linsawati/AP hide caption
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with an alleged spy for China .
Nvidia's National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be responsible for oversight of national security policies and compliance with export controls, the company said Tuesday that the
Nvidia's advanced chips are in high demand because they're essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the artificial intelligence boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China.
The committee will meet at least once every quarter and have three members from Nvidia's board of directors. It will work with independent third-party experts as it oversees efforts to enhance the company’s existing national security and global trade compliance team.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” Chairman Harvey Jones said in a statement.
“President Donald Trump said it was ‘good’ that Nvidia had created a national security and export control oversight committee shortly after arriving in the Philippines on Tuesday evening.
“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said during a photo opportunity in Manila with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan . “It’s a great idea.”
Huang was forced to resign as Nvidia's CEO last week following scrutiny of his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who used to lead Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of the U.S. export controls.
AP writer Darlene Superville in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Deutsche Bank Leak Reveals $582 Million In Epstein Payments, Accidental Trump Tax Disclosure
articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Reveals $582 Million In Epstein Payments, Accidental Trump Tax Disclosure
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - were closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
The damage after the overnight attack, involving missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang started closing the Bank of Nvidia months before he left — here’s what’s still open: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang started closing the Bank of Nvidia months before he left — here’s what’s still open: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia reports Tuesday with its longtime finance chief, Colette Kress , in charge. The Bank of Nvidia she inherited was already turning customers away.
Wall Street will grade Nvidia ( NVDA ) on chips and guidance after the bell . But the most revealing page may sit in the back of the filing, where Nvidia lists what it has promised to pay or guarantee for others.
That list nearly doubled in a single quarter, JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest noted , and comes to about $530 billion with guarantees included. Huang's exit put that web of deals under the microscope.
The man who built the bank had already started closing its windows.
In August, Nvidia's guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center came in at less than half the $250 billion that had been discussed. By the end of the month, Nvidia had paused revenue-sharing deals with neoclouds — upstart cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips — The Wall Street Journal reported . In October, Huang told those partners to get their customers to pay upfront.
"You're not charging what you should be charging," he told them at a conference in Berlin, according to the Journal.
Neoclouds may be rooting for a Huang comeback , but his return wouldn't reopen windows he was shutting himself. Kress is expected to tighten the purse strings even further, the Journal reported. The $500 billion lending platform Nvidia launched with Wall Street in August still hasn't closed a deal, and lenders want Nvidia to back more than a quarter of each loan, Bloomberg reported.
"I do expect the company to pivot pretty hard under new leadership," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. "I think we're going to see less circular financing activity. We've already seen a slowdown just in the last three weeks."
The stock market noticed first. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) have each lost more than half their value in three months, while Nvidia is down about 30%. Nebius is still up for the year.
Some promises can't be taken back. Deals Nvidia already signed — from chip supply orders to cloud capacity it agreed to rent back — are still owed. And Nvidia is set to buy $10 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the AI lab's IPO , which prices Wednesday, according to Anthropic's amended filing.
That makes Tuesday's report about more than demand. Investors will want to know whether the pile of promises keeps growing, and whether Kress sounds like a banker who's still lending.
David Nelson, chief strategist at Belpointe Asset Management, sees two AI trades hiding inside one. Some companies pay for their data centers out of the cash they earn. Others lean on leases, loan guarantees and "other people's money," as he put it, the kind of help Nvidia has been handing out.
"They have been priced as one trade," he wrote Monday. "They won't be much longer."

articles.title_orig: Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption
articles.title_zh: Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption
articles.content_orig:
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he would resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of profiting from a government railway project.
At a press conference, Khurelsukh said he was being "falsely accused and defamed" but would resign in order to "restore my good name."
He has pledged to cooperate with investigators.
Before the resignation takes effect, it must first be accepted by parliament, the State Great Khural.
Nyambaatar Khishgee, the ex-mayor of Ulaanbaatar, the country's capital, on Saturday accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million (around €23 million) linked to the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project.
The railway connects the Tavantolgoi coal mine with the Mongolian port of Gashuunsukhait on the Chinese border, a central hub for the export of coal from Mongolia to China.
The former mayor belongs to the president's party, but is part of a different faction within it.
The opposition Democratic Party picked up on the accusations and called on Khurelsukh to step down.
According to the allegations, Khurelsukh received the money in bribes from the conglomerate Bodi International LLC, which received the contract to construct the railway without a competitive tender.
Bodi on Monday denied having paid any cash bribes to obtain the contract.
Khurelsukh, from the Mongolian People's Party, has been president since 2021.
But infighting has caused disruption in the party in recent years, with three prime ministers taking office in just nine months.
Khurelsukh paid a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 this year.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said were involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of settlement goods and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".
The announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel .
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6: How one school is battling the 'GTA flu' with warnings to parents and prizes for pupils
articles.title_zh: GTA 6: How one school is battling the 'GTA flu' with warnings to parents and prizes for pupils
articles.content_orig:
A school concerned about pupils not coming in on the day the highly-anticipated GTA VI video game is released has offered young people prizes for turning up for classes.
Belfast Boys' Model school issued letters to parents, saying that the release of the game on Thursday coincided with GCSE maths exams.
The school said that "activities such as playing Grand Theft Auto can wait until the weekend".
On Monday, the school added that pupils who attended school on both Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw for a £70 gift card for either PlayStation or Xbox.
In a letter issued to parents, reported by The Nolan Show , the school reminded "all parents and carers of the importance of ensuring that students attend school on Thursday 19th November".
It also said that "all Year 11 students and some Year 12 students" would be sitting a GCSE maths exam on Thursday, the same day the game comes out.
"Good attendance is one of the strongest indicators of academic success," the letter added.
Mary Montgomery, who is principal of the school, said "the primary focus" of her letter was Thursday's Mathematics examination and "encouraging our boys to be in school and ready to achieve their best".
"The results at GCSE have been fantastic in recent years and we want to continue that success for the boys," she said.
"It also highlighted the launch of GTA as something which might entice some boys to stay at home. However, the games vouchers were a pupil-led incentive."
GTA VI is released on Thursday, 13 years after the previous edition and with an estimated development cost of more $1bn (£866m).
In 2013, the term 'GTA Flu' was coined in reference to the large number of sick days reportedly taken when GTA V was released.
On Monday, the school announced that all pupils in attendance on Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw to win one of two £70 gift cards "for PlayStation/Xbox".
The school's head boy said "the idea came from us as pupils".
"We wanted to do something positive to mark International Men's Day and, importantly, to raise money for a charity that supports male victims of domestic violence," he said.
"For us, the most important thing was having as many boys as possible in school so everyone could get involved and support the fundraising."
He added that gaming can help the pupils "switch off and manage some of the stress around exams, which is important with GCSE modules this week".
Speaking to The Nolan Show, a former school principal Kathleen O'Hare said the decision to send the letter to parents was "very wise".
"The cult of this game is so large that parents will be put under extreme pressure at times," she said.
O'Hare added that it has been "proven" that missing a day of school "really does matter".
Pete Wray, a Ulster Unionist Party councillor who works with children, said "there is a sizable amount of young people that are in our education system and completely disengage".
"They take an odd day off, and once they've got one day off, they're anxious about going back because they know they're going to be behind, and that leads to more and more problems," he said.
Wray said he will be imploring young people not to miss school to play the game, but that he "completely understands how people can become engrossed in it".
Considered one of the most highly-anticipated video games in history, the game is the latest in the long-running Grand Theft Auto series.
The game series, which has attracted controversy in the past over its depiction of violence and crime, is also the most expensive game ever made, with estimates putting development costs at more than $1bn (£866m).
The previous game in the series, GTA 5, sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time, which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for developer Rockstar.
GTA 6 will feature its first ever playable female protagonist in a 3D setting - Lucia - alongside her partner in life and crime, Jason, as a second playable character.
Like other GTA games before it, the sixth chapter is set in a fictional US state - this time in Leonida, which is Rockstar's version of Florida.

articles.title_orig: Nike hosts first investor day in 9 years as it tries to rightsize its business
articles.title_zh: Nike hosts first investor day in 9 years as it tries to rightsize its business
articles.content_orig:
Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.
The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.
Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.
The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."
"We're concentrating our resources where we have the greatest potential to win," Nike CEO Elliott Hill said in a statement. "We're also changing how we operate — delivering breakthrough products, building deeper local connections and moving faster to capture demand. Together, these actions are designed to return NIKE to sustainable, profitable growth."
Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.
Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.
Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.
Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.
The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.
Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.
At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.
CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.
The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.
Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

articles.title_orig: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
articles.title_zh: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
articles.content_orig:
Silicon Valley wants its moneymaker-in-chief back.
Jensen Huang, forced to resign from Nvidia last week in the midst of multiple scandals, has found a groundswell of support for his unlikely return. Among the cheerleaders for Huang’s comeback: several prominent Big Tech executives and the president of the United States.
Their desire for his reinstatement is plain: Nvidia is the AI industry’s financier, and Jensen Huang the top dealmaker. Nvidia’s willingness to lend gobs of money to AI companies to help make their massive ambitions possible turned Huang into the king of AI.
Still, some of Huang’s more questionable deals – and his questionable behavior – also put the company at risk.
Huang’s actions punctured massive holes in the myth of his singular and irreplaceable leadership, surfacing some significant preexisting doubts about the viability of the company’s long-term business strategy.
A more conservative Nvidia – one that plays by the rules – may be painful for AI companies that relied on Huang’s risktaking in the near term. But it could set Nvidia and the broader industry on a more sustainable course in the long run.
Around 200,000 signatories of a #standwithjensen open letter argued Huang deserves to come back to Nvidia, at least while an independent investigation continues. Many of the comments defended Huang as indispensable and the linchpin of the AI industry’s success. Nvidia declined to comment.
Huang engendered support from the industry by spearheading complicated financing deals – often called circular financing – that gave many AI companies access to Nvidia’s powerful chips and computing power that they wouldn’t otherwise be able to afford or access.
The amount of money involved in those deals is astounding: Nvidia last quarter listed $164.5 billion in land and power guarantees and AI cloud infrastructure agreements, including $20 billion worth of leases for data centers that haven’t broken ground yet.
Nvidia isn’t just financing small companies: Included in that sum is $105 billion in leases to SB Energy , a company with backing from SoftBank that is building a massive Ohio data center for OpenAI.
In turn, that massive funding secured demand for Nvidia’s own products – and stakes in the companies that bought or leased its chips: Nvidia owns about $3 billion worth of SB Energy’s shares – and $45 billion worth of other companies’ stock.
Huang’s ouster could take $50 billion out of the circular financing system, according to Tim Arcuri, analyst at UBS.
Another risk of Huang’s ouster: New leadership will probably be more cautious about where and with whom it does business, particularly in Southeast Asia.
Huang knew the company needed the region to support Nvidia’s ambitious growth targets. He championed Nvidia’s ability to continue selling its chips to China, despite US export restrictions – ultimately gaining the Trump administration’s support to carve out a path for the company to sell powerful, but not top-tier, AI chips there.
Ironically, Huang’s scandal may put some of Nvidia’s access to the region at risk. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday told Fox News that the company’s international sales merit more scrutiny.
“Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent wondered aloud.
The dynamics of Jensen Huang’s relationship to Megaspeed’s Alice Huang remain uncertain, as is her potential role as a Chinese intelligence asset. But the Singaporean government and US officials have been scrutinizing Megaspeed for potentially reselling Nvidia’s chips to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
Nvidia’s board on Tuesday sait it had established a new national security and export control oversight committee that will meet at least quarterly and ensure the company is abiding by global trade regulations. It will also beef up its internal national security and compliance initiatives. The US Commerce Department on Monday proposed tightened restrictions on sales of high-end AI chips to Singapore following the scandal.
Reduced sales to Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries could risk as much as a 10% reduction to Nvidia’s revenue in the long term, said Arcuri.
Despite those risks, Huang’s ouster may ultimately make for a strong Nvidia.
Those so-called circular financing deals are controversial for a reason: The deals can leave Nvidia on the hook if a borrower defaults, a data center project is severely delayed or demand for AI falls through.
Across the industry, the value of those off-balance-sheet debt obligations, including long-term contracts and lease guarantees, exceeds $3 trillion, said Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr in a speech Monday . He noted rising bond yields for smaller AI companies led to increasingly complex deals that warrant particularly close scrutiny and could mess with the market.
“This financial complexity can be opaque,” Barr said. “That opacity can exacerbate selloffs when investor sentiment shifts, as it is hard to know where risk resides.”
Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress, who is the company’s chief financial officer, had challenged Huang on some of the more audacious funding efforts, including increasingly controversial and highly leveraged neocloud companies, noted Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. He believes Kress, with the support of a more cautious board, will be tempted to rein in some of Nvidia’s riskier financing operations.
Tech bros and President Donald Trump may be advocating for Huang to stick around, but fears about a management shakeup impact on Nvidia are overblown, a number of industry analysts argue. Kress predicted in August that the company’s sales will grow 70% next year, and demand for Nvidia’s AI chips remains so high, the company will maintain a backlog of orders that lasts well into 2028.
“Leadership does matter, particularly when you’re talking about someone as influential as Jensen Huang who has been at the helm for 33 years and is seen as a tech visionary,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. “So this is no joke, but the company certainly is not going out of business from this and investors needed to keep that in mind.”
And it’s not like Huang’s scandals shine a positive light on him and his decision making. Keeping Huang in power (or bringing him back) would have been a bigger risk than letting him walk, said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors.
No one can sustain the hockey stick-like growth Nvidia had exhibited over the past several years. When companies start growing exponentially, that’s when CEOs tend to start grasping at straws for new growth paths – and that’s when they often get into trouble, noted Minow.
So a more discerning Nvidia adds short-term volatility but could put it on the path to greater sustainability.
And it may have a better chance of achieving that without Huang.
“Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean,” said former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein in a post on X . “But as de Gaulle said, ‘The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.’”

articles.title_orig: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
articles.title_zh: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.
GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.
She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".
She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.
And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.
Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.
Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.
Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.
When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing taking several days off to play.
Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.
It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.
"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.
"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.
Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.
But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include  banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.
Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish , show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.

articles.title_orig: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
articles.title_zh: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
articles.content_orig:
Xbox VP of Next Generation Jason Ronald has clarified that Project Helix is "designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games, not a PC that can also play console games."
In the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine , Ronald described Project Helix as "the ultimate gaming machine – one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed."
"The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Project Helix's console and PC compatibility in March, adding that the console will "lead in performance" for Xbox and PC games.
As Ronald previously discussed at GDC Festival of Gaming , Project Helix will utilise neural rendering, which uses AI models to enhance graphics. Ronald identified neural rendering as a particular focus for Project Helix, as it also addresses the ongoing component crisis.
"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and platform designer, it's one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also [making] things accessible and affordable."
"This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower [and] additional memory."
He concluded: "I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last ten years."
Reports last month indicated that Project Helix is expected to launch during the 2028 holiday season , with a projected price between $1,200 and $1,800.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.
The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.
Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.
Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks mostly stabilized from a sell-off that day before. Nvidia shares were up slightly ahead of the start of regular trading in New York.

articles.title_orig: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow? : Planet Money
articles.title_zh: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow? : Planet Money
articles.content_orig:
A cash cow. Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac hide caption
Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?
Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money . By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
Then Google vice president of search Marissa Mayer in 2009. ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion . That's more than a millionfold increase.
Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.
In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.
Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer , a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.
Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."
Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.
If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.
Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.
The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail .
Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.
The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.
Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?
Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages , recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go .
The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.
But they didn't release it.
Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.
Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.
So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?
Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?
His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.
In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.
Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.
"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.
Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist , sexist , and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.
And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.
Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma . Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.
Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.
We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?
Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.
The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.

articles.title_orig: Well-known journalist who reported death threats is gunned down on street in Costa Rica
articles.title_zh: Well-known journalist who reported death threats is gunned down on street in Costa Rica
articles.content_orig:
Costa Rican independent journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who had called out alleged ties between drug traffickers and politicians on social media, was shot dead Monday outside the capital San Jose, authorities said.
Two men riding on a motorcycle opened fire on Rodriguez as he was driving through the town of Santo Domingo de Heredia, police chief Raul Rivera said. Rodriguez was attacked at around 3:20 p.m. local time amid heavy traffic on a main highway, Reuters reported , citing the Red Cross.
Rodriguez, 50, had reported receiving several death threats from drug trafficking groups.
He would name drug lords by their full names and claimed to have provided reports to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration regarding links between drug traffickers and powerful figures in politics and business.
When President Laura Fernandez was running for office last year, she sued Rodriguez for defamation after he posted a video claiming her home had been built with money allegedly provided by a drug trafficker.
"Regardless of the content of his statements, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression," Fernandez said in a video released by her office .
Rodriguez ran for president in 2022, but his nomination was rejected by electoral authorities on technical grounds.
He also accused his ex-wife of being involved in drug trafficking. She has filed a complaint alleging he sexually abused their children.
The Costa Rican Journalists' Association condemned his killing and demanded "a swift investigation."
"All evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica -- a person who published information about organized crime in the country," the association's president, Yanancy Noguera, told AFP.
In recent years, Costa Rica has gone from being a drug transit point to a logistics hub for trafficking, and has lost its status as one of the safest countries in Central America.
Fernandez, who took office in May, campaigned on a promise to crack down on the crime wave, and said she is drawing inspiration from El Salvador's iron-fisted President Nayib Bukele.
Fernandez herself that she has received intelligence reports showing that jailed gang members have ordered her assassination, the Tico Times reported on Monday.
Attorney General Carlo Diaz announced an investigation into the murder, adding that Rodriguez -- who had contributed to various Costan Rican print, radio and television media outlets and more recently turned to social media -- had declined to enter a witness protection program.
Diaz told local media the crime scene resembled a contract killing, Reuters reported.
"We know he was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking," Diaz said. "Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society."
According to Reporters Without Borders , more than half of the world's countries now fall into the "difficult" or "very serious" categories for press freedom.

articles.title_orig: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."
