articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

articles.title_orig: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
articles.content_orig:
Thankfully, the object did not hit his eye or cause serious harm.
A rosary bracelet thrown from the crowd struck Pope Leo XIV in the face Monday, just below his right eye, as he was traveling in the popemobile through the Las Palmas Air Base in Lima.
The incident occurred following a Mass at the conclusion of his apostolic trip to the country that drew nearly 1.5 million people.
Video footage shows Leo XIV ducking immediately after being hit, clearly reacting to the the impact. Thankfully, the object did not strike his eye or cause serious harm. The pope continued his journey without needing medical assistance.
Following the Mass, Pope Leo headed to the Callao Air Base, from where he departed for Rome, bringing an end to his first pastoral visit to South America as the successor of St. Peter.
Throughout his trip through Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, the Holy Father has shown a remarkable ability to catch — on the fly — rosaries, single-decade rosaries, and other religious devotional items that the faithful often toss toward him.
Although these gestures are typically made with affection and devotion, they also entail risks, especially in large crowds and when the popemobile is moving at higher speeds.
The incident calls attention to the danger that such items being thrown at the pope can pose. What may be an expression of affection for many of the faithful can, in fact, become a risk to the physical safety of the pope and those around him.
This story was first published by EWTN News Español, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

articles.title_orig: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
articles.title_zh: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is in Asia for a three-day trip, focusing on trade agreements, regional diplomacy, and discussions on nuclear stockpiles with world leaders.
President Donald Trump is in Asia for a three-day trip, focusing on trade agreements, regional diplomacy, and discussions on nuclear stockpiles with world leaders.
President Donald Trump is in Asia for a three-day trip, focusing on trade agreements, regional diplomacy, and discussions on nuclear stockpiles with world leaders.
The president is currently in the Philippines, where he is meeting with leaders who look to the United States for help in addressing Beijing's aggression in the region. According to the White House, Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand during his visit.
Before that, Trump met with leaders from India, Japan, and Australia. This marks the first time the group, known as the Quad, has convened since Trump began his second term.
"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific. We have outstanding relationships and coordinate closely on matters of regional security, economic security and diplomacy, and we talk quite often," Trump said.
Trump will then travel to China to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit , also known as APEC.
For the final portion of his trip, Trump is scheduled to participate in the first-ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump has indicated that the meeting will primarily focus on nuclear stockpiles, though the leaders are also expected to discuss Iran.
A spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said China’s looking to have in-depth discussions about safeguarding world peace and promoting stability, adding the talks will be of "groundbreaking significance."
Trump administration officials have been trying to downplay the president's relationship with the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, who resigned from the company after admitting he had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.
Despite the administration trying to show distance between Trump and Huang, the former CEO accompanied the president on Air Force One during Trump's last trip to China in May. Huang has also popped up at the White House a few times.
Last week, Trump was asked if he would bring up Huang with President Xi, and he said, "No, I don't think so. I mean, maybe. I'm sure President Xi will ask me about it."
There are a number of people accompanying the president on his trip to Asia this week, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , and Elon Musk.

articles.title_orig: "Essentially Worthless" - Disgruntled Fans Are Review Bombing Pikmin 4 On Switch 2
articles.title_zh: "Essentially Worthless" - Disgruntled Fans Are Review Bombing Pikmin 4 On Switch 2
articles.content_orig:
Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is out now, bringing 4K visuals to the 2023 title along with the new Dandori Academy mode and some neat little extras like voice commands.
We awarded it a score of 7/10 in our review. It's still good – hell, the main Pikmin 4 campaign is possibly the best of the bunch – yet we can't deny our disappointment at the lack of mouse controls and 60fps performance.
But if you take a look on Metacritic , you'd think Nintendo just put out its worst game in years. Although the metascore is sitting at a commendable 83, the game's user score is much, much lower at 2.3. This essentially means its average is 'Generally Unfavourable'. Yeesh.
Most folks just seem disgruntled at the notion that Nintendo is charging for what they perceive to be a very minor upgrade over the original. It's true that a lot of games over the years have received free updates for newer hardware, but Nintendo has opted to charge £7.99 / $9.99 / €9.99 .
"This switch 2 edition is essentially worthless. At worst it's a spit in the face of series fans. $20 AUD for a bunch of recycled content and 4k visuals. They couldn't even be bothered to implement 60fps even though the system could definitely handle it. Such a lazy update, and yet they have the gall to charge $20 AUD."
Meanwhile, another user provided a slightly more measured assessment, stating:
"The Dandori Academy has reused content, half of the maps so far are taken directly from the base game and the other half share the same exact layout. Plus the new card on the title screen looks like an ad, ruins the nice scenery, fortunately it can be hidden.
"The main game has also suffered, now somehow having longer loading times than it did on the original Switch. All other Switch 2 editions have made them shorter, so this is really weird. It's not a small difference either, some have literally doubled."
The comment about the load times is particularly interesting.
This has been highlighted elsewhere, with YouTuber 'Press A!' posting an analysis titled 'Pikmin 4's DLC is a disaster...' (flexing that signature YouTube nuance right there) in which he compares the load times of the Switch 2 Edition with the original. When exiting out of a cave, the original would take around 6 seconds or so to load the main environment, however the same moment took over 30 seconds in the Switch 2 version.
A few people have mentioned the load times being quite long, so we tested it out ourselves. While loading into a cave takes about 6 seconds, loading out took around 14-15 seconds. Not the 30+ that others are citing, then, but probably long enough to raise an eyebrow or two.
Pikmin 4's user score on Switch 2 is a startling contrast to that of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . Despite some concerns here and there regarding the game's overall difficulty and approachability compared to the original, Ocarina of Time commands the highest user score of all time at 9.6.
We'll be curious to see whether Nintendo takes any steps to improve the load times in Pikmin 4, but for what you actually get with the new content and visual enhancements on Switch 2, we'd say the upgrade price is probably appropriate. It'll tide us over until Pikmin 5, at least.

Jensen Huang appears to be accepting that he will not be returning to Nvidia ( NVDA ) as CEO.
At least, that's if you decode the move he just made on his X account.
Huang updated his profile on Tuesday, changing it to simply "founder" of Nvidia. It no longer has the Nvidia affiliation badge.

Reuters reported last Thursday that Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, whose identity has not been disclosed.

articles.title_orig: The new tax plan that could stop Social Security cuts
articles.title_zh: The new tax plan that could stop Social Security cuts
articles.content_orig:
Dane Kelly , Digital Reporter
Nearly 2 million Michigan residents could see their monthly Social Security checks slashed if Congress fails to address the program’s looming funding shortfall.
Under current projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees , the primary Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will exhaust its cash reserves by late 2032. If combined with the disability trust fund, the depletion date extends to mid-2034.
By federal law, Social Security cannot borrow money or pay out more than it collects in revenue. Once the reserves run dry, the system will only be able to fund an estimated 78% to 83% of promised benefits , triggering an automatic, across-the-board cut of up to 24% for retirees, surviving spouses and dependents .
The impact would hit Michigan harder than most of the country.
According to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , Michigan retirees would absorb the ninth-largest dollar reduction in the nation, losing an average of $523 per month -- or roughly $6,276 each year.
Nearly 20% of Michigan’s population relies on these programs and would face reduced benefits.
That loss would strip $12.1 billion annually from the state. That’s 1.6% of Michigan’s gross domestic product, tying the state for the sixth-highest economic impact in the United States .
While demographic pressures have long been cited as the primary driver, recent economic research points to revenue shifts .
A study by the AARP Public Policy Institute found that taxable payroll fell from 41% of U.S. GDP in 1983 to 34% in 2025, largely due to rising wage inequality and a shift toward untaxed investment and business profits.
Today, only 83% of earnings are subject to the payroll tax, down from the 90% target set during the 1983 reforms.
Had taxable payroll kept pace with economic growth, Social Security would have collected an extra $10.8 trillion -- extending full benefits to 2059, according to AARP .
Trustees also cited lower projected immigration levels and tax revenue reductions from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 , which reduced the amount of revenue generated from taxing benefits for upper-income retirees.
Lawmakers on Capitol Hill face several competing proposals to avert insolvency, including lifting or eliminating the payroll tax cap for high earners , expanding taxes to certain investment and business income, raising the overall payroll tax rate or altering retirement ages.
Without legislative intervention before 2032, the reductions will take effect automatically under existing law.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang was building Anthropic's worst nightmare. Then he was ousted.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang was building Anthropic's worst nightmare. Then he was ousted.
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
Jensen Huang 's dramatic departure from Nvidia may be the best thing to happen to Anthropic just as the AI startup prepares to go public this week.
Under Huang, Nvidia was investing heavily in cheaper, more open AI models that compete with Anthropic's offerings. The chip giant was also backing startups developing these alternative models and helping make them widely available.
That threatened Anthropic's business model, which involves spending heavily to develop closed AI models and charges customers to use them, often at higher prices than open alternatives.
"People really need to understand that the 'Cold War' going on here is that Nvidia was on a titanic collision course with the labs," the CEO of a leading AI startup told Business Insider. This person asked not to be identified while discussing sensitive topics.
The executive, who supports the open-source AI community and is sympathetic to Huang, described an ambitious Nvidia strategy to develop its own AI models, invest in rival startups, and build an ecosystem that could challenge not just Anthropic, but OpenAI too.
This strategy was just beginning to come together. But with Huang gone, the threat has diminished considerably.
The timing is extraordinary. Anthropic is preparing for a stock market debut this week that could value it at $1.4 trillion.
Investors are being asked to make an enormous bet on the future profitability of its AI services. Huang was helping build a world in which companies wouldn't necessarily have to pay Anthropic for that intelligence.
The strategy centered on " open-weight " AI models. Unlike Anthropic's Fable and Opus offerings and OpenAI's top GPT models, these alternative systems can be downloaded, modified, and operated independently.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
That makes them attractive to businesses that want greater control over their AI systems without paying a leading AI lab every time someone uses the technology.
Nvidia was pursuing this aggressively.
It developed its own family of open models, called Nemotron. It also backed startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines Lab, and Poolside, while moving to acquire Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing open-weight AI models.
Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang's ouster "an attack on open models" at a Silicon Valley conference on Monday.
"Jensen is the premier champion of open models," Masad said. "If it wasn't for Jensen, there wouldn't be a lot of funding going into US open model companies."
On November 3, I watched Huang evangelize this strategy at a Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco.
He acknowledged the value of closed AI models from companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, but argued that businesses shouldn't have to rely on them. Instead, they could take open-weight models and adapt them to their specific needs, creating AI systems that could be even more powerful.
"By taking an open frontier model, adapting it and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access, your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a super intelligence," Huang told Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao on stage.
"And I think those times are here," he added.
This strategy made business sense for Nvidia. More open models running on its chips meant more potential customers.
It was becoming increasingly important as Anthropic and OpenAI sought alternatives to Nvidia's expensive hardware.
In fact, Anthropic has developed a system that could be Nvidia's worst nightmare, as Business Insider reported in October .
Anthropic disclosed in its IPO filing that it has spent years developing software that allows it to shift AI work between different types of chips from Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and AMD. That gives Anthropic more flexibility to choose the cheapest or most effective chips for a particular task, reducing its dependence on Nvidia and potentially weakening Nvidia's ability to charge premium prices.
The shift is already significant. A November 14 analysis by Michael Cembalest of JPMorgan Asset Management estimated that Nvidia accounted for just 39% of future computing commitments by leading AI labs, down from more than 80% of AI chip revenue in recent years.
There was another key area of AI where Nvidia and Anthropic clashed.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has advocated for very strict limits on advanced US chip sales to China, arguing these restrictions are essential to maintaining America's technological lead.
Huang fought against those restrictions, warning that shutting China out would encourage Chinese companies to develop competing technology.
Now he's gone, Anthropic's worldview is prevailing. On Monday, the US government rolled out new restrictions that close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to use Nvidia GPUs by renting them from data centers outside China.
It's a win for China hawks within the administration and a huge victory for Amodei, arguably the biggest China hawk of them all.
There are caveats. For instance, Nvidia's interim CEO could continue Huang's strategies. Still, the immediate strategic implications are striking.
Anthropic is about to ask investors to bet on its future dominance of AI. Just days before that moment, one of the industry's most powerful figures pushing an alternative vision has been forced out.
For Anthropic, that's enormous.

articles.title_orig: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
articles.title_zh: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue.
The Trump administration on Monday announced it was tightening a loophole that has allowed Chinese tech firms to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing the most advanced A.I. chips through third countries.
The move comes just days ahead of President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in the wake of Nvidia, the creator of the most advanced AI chips, becoming enmeshed in an international scandal that prompted the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang and a fresh round of scrutiny over the company’s ties to China.
The new rule released by the Commerce Department will require that buyers of advanced semiconductors from certain countries will need to secure a license to sell or transfer those chips.The administration said the rule would specifically impact buyers from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, describing those countries as having a “higher than normal” risk of evading current sanctions.
The measure is set to go into effect in 90 days.
China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia. Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports.
The new rule will also give Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wide discretion as to which chips may require more safeguards. According to the rules, the secretary may inform a company selling AI chips “orally” about stricter export rules on certain items if the department believes there is “an unacceptable risk.”
The rules came days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Lutnick for failing to properly oversee the chip exports to China in a CNBC interview on Sunday.
The rare public criticism came after Huang’s resignation as head of Nvidia in the wake of revelations about his extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected by the Commerce Department of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls, but a month-long investigation by the Commerce Department into Megaspeed was halted last year after a top Nvidia official intervened , according to the New York Times.
“Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said on CNBC on Sunday. “But Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
“President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage,” Bessent added.
Both Lutnick and Bessent are expected to travel with Trump to China this week, according to Semafor. Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Aside from AI chips, the first-of-its-kind summit will also focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons.
The federal government began restricting China's access to AI chips in Trump's first term, as both countries raced to become the leader  in this fast-evolving technology. The Biden administration intensified this policy , making the export of advanced chips to China illegal in 2022. Beijing nevertheless still succeeded in stockpiling thousands of chips to build its own AI systems thanks to an international smuggling network.
Last year, Trump reversed his own administration’s export restrictions, allowing Nvidia to sell two types of computer chip used in the development of artificial intelligence to "approved customers" in China in exchange for a portion of the revenue cut. Those moves are poised to draw more scrutiny next year when Democrats take control of Congress, with both chambers likely probing the Trump Administration's AI policies in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Congressional lawmakers have asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as a part of the investigation.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump reported trades this year that suggest he has held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, disclosures that will likely escalate scrutiny into the president’s relationship to the AI giant and his administration’s oversight of an industry at the center of international scandal.
Financial disclosures, reviewed by The Washington Post, revealed that the president’s Nvidia stakes grew sharply from an estimated $615,000 to $1.3 million at the end of 2024 to as much as $62 million within the last year. The latest filings ​do not capture trades from the past two months, meaning that the values could be even higher.
The disclosures follow Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO after the revelation of his extramarital affair with ‌Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , who is accused of having intelligence ties to Beijing.
White House officials have repeatedly maintained that the president does not personally pick or trade individual stocks and Trump has rejected calls to divest his stock holdings. Trump’s assets are in a trust managed by his children and independent financial managers handle his portfolio, according to the White House.
But enormous growth of the president’s financial stakes in Nvidia are in parallel to the president’s close relationship to Jensen Huang and the administration’s regulatory moves that have opened the door for the company to do business in China. The president has routinely defended his administration against criticism over export controls that appear to have been lucrative for both Nvidia and the president.
Nvidia’s stock is trading at roughly $157.72, down over 3.1 percent on the day, as investors react to Huang’s blockbuster resignation ahead of a third-quarter earnings call scheduled for Tuesday.
The company’s board, however, is not considering bringing him back, according to CNBC.
Huang’s resignation last week followed news of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials have suspected Alice Huang of spying for China, and the Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed breached U.S. export restrictions.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined Alice Huang had been recruited to influence Jensen Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
Trump, however, appeared to cast doubt on his own administration’s assessment.
“I don’t know that she’s a spy at all. Nobody's proven that,” he told reporters outside the White House on Monday.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy,” he said.
“Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” he continued, “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t.”
According to The New York Times , State Secretary Marco Rubio drafted a classified memorandum on Alice Huang’s alleged scheme and had even briefed the president about her suspected activities while the pair were traveling to China on Air Force One in May — months before Jensen Huang’s admission of the affair.
But Trump reportedly brushed the warnings aside and maintained his relationship with the tech mogul, who frequently appeared at the White House and donated $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
Asked on Monday whether he trusted the intelligence that Rubio reportedly provided him, Trump appeared to suggest he thought the reporting was false.
“Who told me that?” he told reporters. “I haven’t heard that.”
Congressional watchdogs are eager to dive into the president’s stocks and his administration’s policies surrounding AI and Nvidia, which include easing Biden-era export restrictions on American AI chips to China in May 2025. That decision opened the door for Nvidia to sell its chips to approved Chinese customers later that year, with a portion of revenue to the U.S. government.
In December, Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to approved customers in China, with 25 percent of the revenue going to the U.S.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this summer whether the government should investigate Trump’s purchase of as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock — just one week before the Commerce Department formalized those export restrictions. Bessent responded by suggesting that Congress should look into banning its own members from stock trading before looking to the White House.
Trump has sought to diffuse tension among his Cabinet officials in wake of the scandal, following reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick prevented U.S. oversight on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.
That reportedly escalated to a Situation Room showdown between Lutnick and Bessent, who appeared to put the blame on the Commerce chief during an appearance on CNBC last week.
The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all “were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told the network.
Notably not on that list: Commerce Department.
Trump, however, appeared to acknowledge that Lutnick likely resisted putting Megaspeed — seen as a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls — on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
“He was doing that because you could have — if you didn’t delay it, If you didn’t do something — you could have a blow up with China,” Trump said Monday. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I’ll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides.”
Republican and Democratic members of Congress, meanwhile, are jockeying for Jensen Huang to testify before several committees.

articles.title_orig: How stingless bees in Peru became the world’s first insects to be granted legal rights
articles.title_zh: How stingless bees in Peru became the world’s first insects to be granted legal rights
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet Initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.
You might not have heard of stingless bees, but there are more than 600 species of them on the planet. Although some measure just 5 millimeters long, they are vital pollinators and last year in Peru, they became the first insects in the world to be granted legal rights.
The Declaration of Rights of Amazonian Stingless Bees, passed by two municipal governments, included the right to exist and thrive, the right to a healthy environment and the right to representation for the bees. It came after tireless campaigning by a coalition of environmental organizations, conservationists and Indigenous groups.
This photographer spent 396 days in the Amazon
Peru has more than 175 species of stingless bees, and they are considered a pillar of the rainforest ecosystem. For years, environmental and Indigenous advocates issued warnings about the rapid decline of their populations, due to deforestation, pesticides and climate change.
Rosa Vásquez Espinoza — a chemical biologist , author and founder of environmental nonprofit Amazon Research Internacional — along with her partner organizations, proposed legislation that would grant rights to the tiny pollinators. Espinoza’s pioneering work resulted in her being named a 2026 Rolex Awards Laureate.
Despite their name, stingless bees do have stingers — but their stings are either reduced or nonfunctional and cannot be used for self-defense. Instead, some species buzz loudly and bite to protect their nests, which are typically found in hollow tree trunks, in the ground or in other crevices, including human-made structures.
Espinoza began researching stingless bee species in 2020 but over time, her work evolved to include more than just a scientific approach.
“When we started our project, we learned that stingless bees were nowhere to be found in the law in Peru, yet they are the native species of Peru,” Espinoza said.
“Stingless bees have the right to be alive, to have access to a healthy flora, free of contaminants, pesticides or (invasive) species,” Espinoza said. “Stingless bees cannot defend themselves in court or against the threats they’re facing. But we as people can give voice to the voiceless.”
In recent years, there has been a growing international movement to recognize the rights of nature, including a successful 2022 campaign to grant legal personhood to the Mar Menor Lagoon ecosystem in Spain and to Peru’s Marañón River in 2024.
Inspired by those successes, the team designed the declaration to include rights for stingless bees to exist without pollution, climate change or human activity impacting their populations.
A collaboration between Amazon Research Internacional and global environmental law nonprofit the Earth Law Center, alongside local stakeholders EcoAsháninka, an organization representing thousands of Indigenous Peruvians, Reserva Comunal Ashaninka and Asociación de Meliponicultores Región Loreto, developed the declaration and pushed for its passage in two provinces, Satipo and Nauta , in October 2025 and January 2026, respectively.
Now, groups like Espinoza’s nonprofit and Indigenous Asháninka leaders will be able to raise violations of the bees’ rights in Peruvian courts.
Protector of the pink dolphins: Fernando Trujillo’s quest to save aquatic life in the Amazon
Constanza Prieto Figelist, the Latin America legal director at the Earth Law Center, said the legislation combined Espinoza’s scientific expertise with wisdom from the Asháninka people, serving as a connection across science, Indigenous culture and government.
“Since the beginning, we have been working with the communities — and so building this relationship with the community and translating this knowledge in a document can be a bridge,” said Figelist.
“I like to see it as a translation of Indigenous perspectives into the legal framework — the idea that nature is alive,” Espinoza said.
According to Espinoza, the declaration of rights will also support the Asháninka people, who have traditionally protected the bees and rely on their pollination to help produce food and medicinal plants, as well as using their honey in traditional medicine.
Figelist said the next step for the team is to implement an action plan for the new legislation.
Espinoza’s organization, the Asháninka people and the local municipal governments are working together to translate the insects’ rights into enforcement. She added that the stakeholders will need to determine when and how the rights outlined in the declaration are violated — for example, the penalty for chopping down a tree that’s home to a protected beehive.
Espinoza hopes the municipal government will approve these regulations this year. Both she and Figelist emphasized the importance of the collaboration between their team and the municipal government.
Figelist emphasized that this legislation is a “first step” for the long-term protection of the bee species.
“We cannot just expand — we need to really settle the basis of implementation first,” Figelist said.
Other provinces in Peru interested in the legislation have since contacted Espinoza’s team, and two municipalities in the Cuzco Region, Pichari and Unión Ashaninka, have approved it as local law.
Espinoza said the team has also heard from organizations from 14 countries across six continents who want to use similar laws to protect their own native bee species.
No court cases involving the law have been heard to date, she said, but added she’d already seen proactive efforts by Peruvian authorities and local communities. These include conducting workshops to expand stingless bee conservation and beekeeping; integrating stingless bees into curricula in schools; and establishing local markets to boost the livelihoods of Indigenous people protecting stingless bees.
“It gives me a lot of hope that we can be a lot more intentional and integrative of our approaches,” Espinoza said. “We don’t just have a shiny win, but long-term, sustained efforts.”

articles.title_orig: N. Korea's Kim inspects tourism development site near China ahead of Trump's Asia trip
articles.title_zh: N. Korea's Kim inspects tourism development site near China ahead of Trump's Asia trip
articles.content_orig:
Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.title_zh: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he may meet with N. Korean leader in China
articles.title_zh: Trump says he may meet with N. Korean leader in China
articles.content_orig:
Trump's trip comes amid the Nvidia CEO scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.

articles.title_orig: South Korea cheating scandal: Are AI smart glasses a threat to exams?
articles.title_zh: South Korea cheating scandal: Are AI smart glasses a threat to exams?
articles.content_orig:
South Korea is racing to fix potential security gaps in upcoming exams after a top scorer on a national test admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat.
Prime Minister Han Seok-sook called an emergency meeting on Monday, where the education minister was tasked with enforcing new anti-cheating measures ahead of high-pressure annual national college entrance exams known as “Suneung” this week.
The scandal began after speculation mounted over a student’s near-perfect scores on two separate exams that contained hundreds of questions.
Now, authorities say cheaters using high-tech gadgets could face criminal prosecution if caught.
In a statement last week, the prime minister said her government “will prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably”.
In a video published online on Sunday, the student, wearing a mask, admitted to using a miniature camera and AI during the exam for aspiring tax accountants.
Identified as Han Won-seok by South Korean media, the student had taken exams in April and July and answered nearly all questions correctly, raising concerns about potential cheating and prompting investigations.
“I cheated using electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not the result of fair effort,” he said in the YouTube video.
He explained that he took photos of the exam questions with the mini camera and sent them to an AI tool. He also said he used a smartphone.
The student said he had submitted a written confession detailing his process to the Seoul police. He also warned future cheaters to reconsider.
“I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught,” he said.
The prime minister has called for his results to be invalidated and for him to be banned from national examinations.
The case has triggered uproar in South Korea, where notoriously difficult tests determine students’ life trajectories.
Many spend much of their high school years preparing to pass entrance exams, particularly the Suneung, or the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), which lasts for nearly 10 hours. Flights are suspended to allow total concentration during the exam’s English listening segment, and drivers are asked not to honk for the half-an-hour it takes.
On Monday, Minister of Education Choi Kyo-jin said new measures would be instituted, including the inspection of glasses worn by students.
He also said cheating with smart devices could carry criminal punishment.
The ministry has in recent weeks said it would pursue criminal prosecution for cheating during the annual college entrance exam. It also said it was seeking to extend the one-year exam ban for those caught using smart devices to three years.
There will be “a thorough inspection of all glasses in each test session to ensure a fair and safe testing environment”, the minister said.
The case has revealed the risks AI could pose to exams as smart gadgets make cheating easier, and as authorities appear to be playing catch-up on how the new tools are being deployed.
It could especially affect Asian countries like South Korea, reputed for conducting arduous exams with strict anti-cheating protocols meant to ensure fairness.
Reports of students using AI-powered smart glasses that allow them to look at questions and see responses immediately are becoming common.
A South Korean education official said students likely enter AI prompts beforehand and activate the glasses during tests.
Early iterations of smart glasses featured identifiable cameras in their frames, but the devices are increasingly inconspicuous, making them difficult to detect.
In October, three students in South Korea were caught using smart glasses during tests at universities in Seoul.
In Taiwan, the National Taiwan University disqualified a student in June from medical school entrance exams for allegedly using AI smart glasses to cheat.
Authorities are promising stricter measures. In July, South Korea’s education authorities banned smart glasses from exams and said they will deploy one dedicated person per 1,312 CSAT test sites to inspect eyewear.
Seoul is also mulling introducing technology to detect advanced gadgets on students, including radio-frequency detectors. Public Wi-Fi, officials say, could be disabled at test sites too.
Chinese authorities are likewise tightening measures for the competitive college entry, or Gaokao, exam by equipping testing sites with intelligent security gates to detect smart glasses and other gadgets.

articles.title_orig: South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Songpa-gu in Seoul will deploy dedicated transport vehicles Thursday to support students taking the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test, the district office announced.
This year's CSAT will run from 8:40 a.m. to 5:45 p.m. Thursday, with 9,550 students sitting the exam across 16 test sites in the district.
A total of 43 marked transport vehicles will be deployed across the district, stationed near major subway stations, bus stops and chronically congested intersections close to test sites.
The district will also step up on-site management to keep traffic moving around test venues. During the morning commute, 178 personnel — including civil servants and members of a model drivers' association — will be posted at key access points around all 16 sites. A 200-meter radius around each venue will be designated an intensive illegal parking enforcement zone, with fines and towing applied to any vehicle blocking exam-takers from entering or exiting.
Noise control will also be tightly managed. From 1:10 p.m. to 1:35 p.m., when the English listening section is administered, all sources of noise near test sites — including road excavation, construction work and large-scale events — will be prohibited.
Songpa-gu District Mayor Seo Gang-seok said all relevant agencies and departments would work together to minimize any inconvenience students might face during transit and ensure they could focus solely on the exam. Seo also urged residents to cooperate with traffic and noise-control measures to help create a safe testing environment.
Meanwhile, Songpa-gu will hold a college admissions briefing for parents of first- and second-year high school students on Dec. 16 at 10 a.m. in the district office's main auditorium. The session will cover upcoming changes to the 2028 college admissions system, including the introduction of a unified CSAT format that eliminates elective subjects in Korean, mathematics and the inquiry areas, and a shift in high school grade reporting from a nine-tier system to a five-tier system.

articles.title_zh: Apec and Asean summits live: protests await Trump in Manila, as Xi greets leaders in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.
